summary: A free course on the scams and account takeovers built for Filipino students, freelancers and jobseekers: fake job offers, task scams, OTP phishing, cloned pages, SIM swap, lending apps that harvest your contacts, and the slow approach that ends at an investment platform. lessons.title: What they are actually after
lessons.content_mdx:
# What they are actually after

Jomar is 22, in his third year at a state university in Cavite, and there is about ₱340 sitting in his e-wallet. When a classmate warned him about scam texts he laughed. There is nothing in the account. Why would anybody bother.

Two weeks later somebody was borrowing money from his blockmates in his name, in his own chat style, from his own account.

Nobody was ever after his ₱340.

## Four things worth taking from a person with no savings

**A code.** The short number that arrives on your phone when something important is about to happen. That code is not information. It is an action waiting to be authorised, and whoever hears it performs the action.

**A password.** Your email password before any other, for the reason below.

**A document.** A photo of your ID. A selfie holding that ID beside your face. A payslip. A signed form. These are not paper. They are what somebody uses to open things in your name.

**A permission.** An app you let read your contacts. An account you let something post from. A person you let onto your screen during a call. You granted each of these once, in a hurry, and never looked at them again.

None of the four needs you to have money.

## Email is not one account, it is the master key

Sit with this until it is uncomfortable.

Whoever controls your mailbox can press "forgot password" on every other account you own, receive the link, set a new password, and lock you out of your own life. Your wallet. Your bank. Your school portal. Your freelancing profile. Every one of them is reachable from the mailbox that receives the resets.

So there is no such thing as protecting your bank account while your email password is the one you also used on a forum years ago. The bank is a room. The mailbox is the front door and the spare key under the mat.

Answer this before you read on: which mailbox would a stranger have to take, in order to take everything else?

## Why a real account is worth more than an empty one

Jomar's account had something his ₱340 did not. It had history. Years of posts. Blockmates who know the name. A way of typing that his friends recognise.

That is the product. A message asking for an emergency ₱1,500 works when it comes from a face people trust, and does not work at all from a blank profile made yesterday. What gets stolen is not your money. It is your ability to be believed, and it gets spent on the next person.

Which means the damage from your account being taken lands mostly on other people. Hold on to that, because it changes what you do in the first hour after it happens. Chapter three covers that hour.

## Why a jobseeker and a freelancer are easier to reach

Here is the uncomfortable part of the job search. It trains you to do the exact thing this course will tell you not to do.

You send your CV to strangers. You attach an ID because onboarding asked for it. You send a selfie holding that ID because a verification step said so. You give an account name and number so that payroll can pay you. You do all of it before you have met anybody, because that is what applying looks like now, and a person three months without work does it faster and questions it less.

So when a fake recruiter asks, nothing feels wrong. The request has the same shape as every real one you answered this month. Chapter two takes that apart properly. For now, notice only this: what you are asked for is exactly what a real employer also asks for, which is why the play works at all.

## Your four, written down

Take ten minutes and write these somewhere offline. A notebook is fine.

1. **Which mailbox holds my resets.** Write the actual address. If there is more than one, write them all, including the abandoned one from high school that is still sitting somewhere as a backup.
2. **Which number receives my codes.** The number attached to your bank, your wallet, and your main accounts.
3. **Which documents are already out there.** Scroll your sent messages. Every ID photo, selfie with ID, payslip and signed form you have sent in the past year, and who you sent it to.
4. **Which apps hold permissions.** The ones that can reach your contacts, your gallery, your messages, or post using your name.

Do not fix anything yet. This is an inventory. You cannot defend what you have never listed.

Item three is the one that makes people go quiet. That is the correct reaction, and the rest of this course is what to do about it.

lessons.title: How the approach starts
lessons.content_mdx:
# How the approach starts

"Hi po, is this Ma'am Cecil? Sorry, wrong number."

Rhea replied because she is polite. That is the whole opening. Being polite.

She is 26, a virtual assistant in Iloilo, and by the time this ends she will have given away more about herself than any form ever asked her for. We will come back to her.

Approaches arrive on every channel you already use, and they move at one of two speeds.

## Fast: it needs an answer today

A text with a link about a parcel held for a fee. A message from a friend on Messenger whose account is no longer being driven by your friend. A Marketplace buyer who is very keen and wants to sort out one thing before paying. A reply to a job application that came back far quicker than any real one. A helpful stranger under the public post where you asked for help, offering to fix it in private. A call about a delivery you are half expecting, or about a transfer you never made.

Fast approaches are built for the minute you are distracted. Riding a jeep. Between classes. Holding a crying baby. They need you inside a few minutes, before you check anything, which is why every one of them supplies a reason that checking would be expensive.

## Slow: it is willing to spend months

Rhea's wrong number became a conversation. He was Filipino, working in Singapore, back home in November. He asked about her clients. He remembered that her mother had an operation coming. Good morning messages landed before her alarm did.

For seven weeks he asked for nothing.

That is not the absence of a scam. That is the first stage of one. Nothing is requested because the request has to arrive after you would defend the person making it.

Around week seven he mentioned, in passing, something he puts money into on the side. He did not offer it to her. He changed the subject. She asked him about it two days later.

That inversion is the craft. When you do the asking, you defend the decision afterwards as your own.

## The pipeline has a name

Romance to investment. The relationship is the setup and a platform is the close, and it is the same machine whether the platform trades currencies, shares or something on a chain.

Where the money question belongs is not here. Whether a promised return can be real is Basic Finance, in its lesson on how the scams are built. Whether a chain makes any of it worse is Basic Blockchain. This lesson stays on the three parts this course owns: the relationship, the isolation, and what you handed over on the way.

Count what Rhea handed over in seven weeks without being asked once. Her birthday. Her mother's maiden name, from a joke about her full name. Her high school. The name of her first dog. The street her boarding house is on. Her biggest client. A photo of her ID, sent the evening he offered to help her sign up for something.

Those are not trivia. Read them again as the answers to somebody's security questions.

## Five tells that work without hearing the story

You will not always recognise the particular scam. You do not have to.

1. **Time pressure.** A window that closes today, and closes for you specifically.
2. **A move to a private channel.** From a comment thread into DMs. From a platform's messages into a separate app.
3. **A reason not to tell anybody.** Keep it between us. Your family will not understand this. Your co-workers will only want in.
4. **A script that survives every question.** Asking questions feels like checking, and it is not. Smooth answers mean the answers have been given many times before.
5. **An offer that found you.** You were not looking for it. It arrived.

Any one of them is worth a pause. Three of them together is the answer.

## The counter-move, which is one sentence

Take it out of the conversation and into tomorrow.

The pressure only works while you are still inside the thread. Step out of it and the offer either survives the night or it does not, and which of those happens is the information you came for. Nothing legitimate collapses because you put your phone down.

The second move undoes the isolation: say it out loud to one person who is not in the conversation. That is what happened to Rhea. She told her ate on a Sunday, and her ate asked one question she could not answer. What is the company called, and where do I look it up.

Rhea never got an answer to that, which was the answer.

## Before the next lesson

Think of the last message that made you feel hurried. Which of the five tells was in it?

lessons.title: Check it before you type
lessons.content_mdx:
# Check it before you type

One sentence carries most of this lesson.

**You never arrive at a login page through a link somebody sent you.**

Not a link in a text. Not a link in an email. Not a link in a chat. Not a QR code. Not the first thing in a search result when you were in a hurry.

Read it again, because everything below is only the reasons.

## The costumes

Invent a bank for a moment. Call it Pilipinas Savings, living at pilipinassavings.com.ph.

**The near miss.** pilipinassavings.com.ph becomes pilipinassavlngs.com.ph. A lower case L where an i used to be. You do not read addresses, you recognise them, and recognition is the thing being used against you.

**The arrangement.** pilipinassavings.com.ph.account-secure.example/login. Every character of the real name is present and correctly spelled, and it is still not the bank. An address is read from the right, and you stop at the first single slash. Walk left from that slash. Skip the ending, which is .com, or .net, or .ph, or .com.ph, or .gov.ph. The very next word going left is the name that decides whose computer answers you. Here the ending is .example, used because it is reserved for teaching and cannot be registered against you, and the next word going left is account-secure. That is whose site this is, and a real one would carry an ordinary ending in that slot. Everything further left, pilipinassavings.com.ph included, is decoration the owner chose and can set to anything at all. Run the same walk on the genuine address and it comes out the other way: in pilipinassavings.com.ph/login the ending is .com.ph and the next word going left is pilipinassavings, which is the bank.

**The advertisement.** A paid slot can sit above the real result in a search. Paying for a slot is not a background check.

**The QR code.** A square you cannot read before you follow it. On a poster at a terminal, on a receipt, on a sticker pasted over the sticker that used to be on a payment counter, or dropped into a chat. Scanning is typing a link you never got to read.

**The lookalike listing.** In an app store, an app with a familiar icon and a name a word or two off.

**The sender name.** The name printed above a message is a label. Labels get set. When a message lands inside the same thread as your real alerts, that tells you the label matched, not that the sender did.

**The caller ID.** The same trick, for calls. The name or number on your screen is a claim about who is calling, nothing more.

## What a padlock actually says

This is the one that catches careful people.

A padlock means the connection between you and whatever computer answered is encrypted. It says nothing at all about who that computer belongs to. Anybody who sets up a site can have one, and a criminal setting up a fake login page sets one up too.

The padlock is a sealed envelope. It does not tell you the address on the front is the right address.

## The replacement habit: a route you chose

Do not get better at judging links. Stop using them.

- Type the address yourself.
- Open your own bookmark, saved on a day when nobody was hurrying you.
- Open the app you installed yourself.
- Ring the number printed on the back of your own card, or on a page you navigated to yourself.

Notice that none of this asks you to spot anything. That is exactly why it works. You cannot be fooled by a link you did not follow, no matter how good it was.

And the message might be real. Often it is. That changes nothing. Act on it through your own route. If your account really has been locked, it will still be locked when you get there by yourself, and it will take you an extra minute.

## For voice: the callback rule

The rule for a phone call has one moving part. You end the call.

Hang up. Wait a moment. Dial a number you sourced yourself. Never a number the caller reads out to you, and never "hold on, let me transfer you", because a transfer keeps you inside the call you are trying to leave.

Knowing your name, your branch, or a recent purchase is not proof of anything. Details leak. Being able to survive you hanging up and calling back is what proof looks like, and if hanging up is presented to you as risky, that is your answer.

## One free alarm you may already own

A password manager fills your login by matching the address it saved. So when it sits there and does not offer to fill, that is not a glitch. It is telling you that the page in front of you is not at the address it knows. People override it because they are in a hurry, and overriding it is the move the fake page is waiting for. A manager can also fail to fill for dull reasons, a login moved to a new address or a form it has not seen before, so treat it as a stop sign and not a verdict. Read the address in the bar before you type anything. If it is the address you expected, type the password in by hand this once, then fix the saved entry afterwards.

Chapter three is where you pick one and move your accounts onto it.

## Before the next lesson

Bookmark three things now, from addresses you typed yourself: your mailbox, your bank or wallet, and the one account you would most hate to lose. Reach each of them once through the bookmark.

That is your route from now on, and you built it on a calm afternoon rather than during somebody else's emergency.

quiz.prompt: It is close to midnight and Jomar gets a Messenger message from Katrina, a blockmate since first year. Her lola has been rushed to hospital and she needs ₱2,000 tonight, to be paid back on Friday. The account is definitely hers: the same profile photo, and years of their old conversations sitting right above the new message. What is the move?

options.text: Reply in the thread with a question only the real Katrina could answer, such as their first year adviser's name.
Ask her onto a video call before he sends anything, since a stranger driving her account could not manage one.
Ring Katrina on the number he already has for her, and treat the request as unanswered until she picks up.
Send nothing tonight and ask two blockmates in the morning whether the story about her lola is true.

quiz.explanation: Nobody here sends money, so that is not what the question is about. Whoever holds the account holds the history, which means a question about first year is answered by scrolling up, and every reply lands in the channel the attacker is driving. A video call is met with a broken camera, a bad signal, or a face he was not expecting. Waiting until morning to ask blockmates spreads the story around without ever reaching Katrina, and it leaves the request live all night. The only check that means anything is a second channel Jomar chose: a number he already had, dialled by him. If she picks up and knows nothing about it, he has also just found out her account is gone, which is worth more to her than the ₱2,000.

quiz.prompt: Divine gets an email saying her wallet account needs re-verification within 48 hours or transfers will be paused. Nothing about it looks wrong: her name is spelled correctly, the logo is right, and there is a button to finish the process. She has genuinely been meaning to update her details, so this may well be real. What should she do?

options.text: Ignore the button, open the wallet app she installed herself, and see whether the same notice is waiting inside it.
Ignore the button, and reply to the email asking support to confirm the message really did come from them.
Ignore the button, and check the sender address against an older receipt from the same wallet company before deciding.
Ignore the button, and search for the wallet's login page instead, using the first result that comes back.

quiz.explanation: The message may be perfectly genuine, and it still does not matter, because arriving by her own route costs Divine a minute when it is real and saves her everything when it is not. Not using the button is only half of it. The other half is where she goes instead. A reply reaches whoever sent the message, so a confirmation by reply confirms nothing. A sender address is a label that can be set, and matching it against an old receipt tests the label rather than the sender. A search result is not a route she chose either, since a paid slot can sit above the real one. The app she installed herself is the only one of the four that nobody else could have arranged for her, and if the notice is real it will be waiting there.

quiz.prompt: A page opens with the logo and layout Arnel expects from his bank, whose real address is pilipinassavings.com.ph. The address in the bar reads pilipinassavings.com.ph.account-secure.example/login. He checks the bank's name letter by letter and every character is correct. Why is this still not his bank?

options.text: There are too many dots in it, and a genuine bank address does not carry more than one of them anywhere.
It probably is his bank, since every character of the bank's name appears in the address and is correctly spelled.
It is his bank as long as the padlock is showing, since a padlock is only issued to the company named in it.
Walking left from the slash and past the ending, the owner is account-secure, and the bank's name is decoration.

quiz.explanation: An address is read from the right, and you stop at the first single slash. Walk left from there, skip the ending, and the very next word is the one that decides whose computer answers you. Here the ending is .example and the next word going left is account-secure, so that is whose site this is. Everything further left is the owner's to arrange however he likes, which is how the bank's name came to be spelled perfectly inside somebody else's address. Counting dots is not the rule: pilipinassavings.com.ph carries two of its own, and Philippine addresses on .com.ph and .gov.ph routinely carry more. The correct spelling is the point of the costume rather than evidence against it. A padlock is about encryption and not about identity. In practice you do not want to be parsing addresses under pressure at all, which is why the habit is to reach a login through a bookmark or the app instead.

quiz.prompt: Doing the inventory from lesson one, Kaye finds a chat thread from eight months ago. In it she sent a photo of the front of her ID, a selfie holding it beside her face, and a filled-in form carrying her signature, to a recruiter who then stopped replying and later deleted the account. What is the honest situation now?

options.text: Deleting the thread on her side removes the copies, so she should clear it now and treat the matter as closed.
Those copies left her hands permanently, so the useful move now is watching for anything opened in her name.
An ID photo cannot be used for anything without the physical card in hand, so there is nothing here to act on.
Since the recruiter deleted the account, whatever they held went with it and her exposure ended there.

quiz.explanation: A document you sent is a copy somebody else now owns. Deleting your side of a thread removes your copy and nothing else, and an account being deleted says nothing about what was saved off it months earlier. The combination Kaye sent is the strong one: an ID, a selfie proving a face goes with it, and a signature. That set is built for opening things in somebody's name. The physical card is not required for that. So the realistic response is not to undo it, which cannot be done, but to stop treating a surprise notice or an unfamiliar account as spam, and to change what she sends next time and at what stage. Chapter two covers who collects this and how, and chapter three covers what to do the hour you find out something was opened.

quiz.prompt: Rhea has been messaging someone for seven weeks after a wrong number text. He has asked her for nothing at all. Last night he mentioned in passing a platform he puts money into on the side, then changed the subject, adding that he does not usually talk about it. Rhea messaged him two days later asking him to explain it. What is the tell she should be reading?

options.text: That he has asked for nothing in seven weeks, which is unusual enough to suggest his interest in her is real.
That the returns sound too good, which is a question for somebody who understands investing.
That he would not come on a video call last month, which is the single test that settles whether a person is real.
That she did the asking, and that a reason to keep it quiet was attached before any money came up.

quiz.explanation: Seven weeks with no request is not evidence of good intentions; it is the cost of the setup, paid so that the request arrives after you would defend the person making it. The inversion is the craft: he mentioned it and stopped, she chased it, and now the decision feels like hers to defend. Secrecy attached to something before money is even discussed is the isolation being installed early. A video call is not a test that settles anything, and a bad one is easily explained away. Whether the returns can be real is a genuine question and it belongs to Basic Finance, which teaches where a promised return has to come from; if it ends up on a chain, Basic Blockchain has that. What Rhea owns right now is the relationship, the secrecy, and what she has already given away.

quiz.prompt: Arnel's phone rings and the screen shows his bank's name. The caller knows his full name and the branch where he opened the account, and says a transfer is being blocked right now and she needs to confirm a few things with him. He tells her he will ring back. Which number should he ring?

options.text: The number sitting in his recent calls list, since that is the number the bank has just been ringing him from.
The number printed on the back of the card in his wallet, which he has carried since the day it was issued.
The direct line she read out to him before he hung up, since he is the one placing the call this time.
The number that comes back first when he searches for his bank's name and the word hotline.

quiz.explanation: Ending the call is the easy half and every option here does it. The callback rule has two moving parts, and the second one is that the number is one he sourced himself. Caller ID is a claim, so the number in his recent calls list is that claim written down, and dialling it dials whatever was displayed. A direct line read out by the caller is the caller's number whichever end places the call, and being invited to ring it back is the script anticipating him. A search result is not a number he sourced, since a paid slot can sit above the real one and a hotline is exactly the search somebody would buy. The card in his wallet was printed by the bank and has been in his pocket since before this call started. Knowing his branch proves nothing either, because details leak and get bought.

quiz.prompt: At a small shop in Cubao the counter has a printed QR code taped to it for payments. Bea notices the sticker looks newer than the laminated sign behind it and is slightly crooked. The cashier is busy and there is a queue behind her. What should she do?

options.text: Skip the code, open the wallet app she installed herself, and pay to the shop's own details or in cash.
Skip the code and pay in cash now, then scan it at home later to find out where it actually pointed.
Skip the code for the moment, and scan it only once the cashier has confirmed the sticker is the shop's own.
Skip the code, and pay through the link on the shop's Facebook page, which she can find while she queues.

quiz.explanation: A QR code is a link you cannot read until you have already followed it, so scanning one is the same act as tapping a link a stranger sent, and it is no safer at home on the sofa than at the counter. A busy cashier does not necessarily know what is taped to the counter, and asking a queue-pressured stranger to vouch for a sticker is not verification. A page she finds while queueing is a route somebody else could have arranged for her, which is the whole lesson. The queue itself is the time pressure, working exactly as intended. Paying through an app she opened herself removes the question rather than answering it.

quiz.prompt: Bea's inventory turns up a photo filter app she installed two years ago and has not opened since. When she installed it she allowed it to reach her contacts and to post using her account. She is about to move on to the next item, since she does not use the app any more. What is worth understanding here?

options.text: An app that is never opened cannot do anything, so a permission sitting on a dormant app carries no real risk.
A permission expires on its own after a long enough stretch of no use, which has already happened in this case.
The access carries on working whether she opens the app or not, and it reaches her contacts and her name.
Removing the app from her phone withdraws every permission she granted it, the posting access included.

quiz.explanation: A permission is standing access, not something that runs only while you are looking at an app. Nobody has to open anything for a granted permission to keep being useful, and it does not lapse because you lost interest. That matters here because of what she granted: her contact list, which is a route to other people, and the ability to post using her name, which is the borrowed trust from lesson one. Deleting an app from a phone removes the app, and access that was granted to an account can outlive it, which is why the two have to be checked separately. This is why the inventory has a fourth item at all. Chapter two picks up what to do with the permissions you find.

lessons.title: What a fake recruiter is collecting
lessons.content_mdx:
# What a fake recruiter is collecting

Marilou is 22, in Tacloban, and has been applying for home based encoding work for a month. A recruiter replies within the hour. Two friendly messages later she is told she got the job. Then the onboarding pack arrives: a photo of her ID front and back, a selfie holding that ID beside her face, her bank account name and number, a copy of her last payslip, and a form to sign with several fields left blank.

Nobody asks her for a single peso.

That is the version worth teaching, because the one with a fee is the easy one. Basic Finance already holds that rule flat, that an employer pays you and you do not pay an employer whatever the fee is called, and it covers the task scam that pays you small amounts before asking you to top up. This lesson is about the recruiter who wants no money at all. What they are collecting is you.

## What each document opens

**The ID photo, front and back.** On its own it is a picture of a card. It is also enough to start an application in your name at a service that never sees you in person.

**The selfie holding it.** This is the one to guard. The document and your face together are what a live person check is built around, so the pair turns a picture of a card into a claim that you were there and agreed.

**The bank or wallet account name and number.** Presented as where your salary will go. It is also a destination somebody else can name, and a detail that makes the next message you receive sound like it came from inside your bank.

**The payslip or certificate of employment.** Your employer, your salary, your employee number, your signature block, and a clean template to copy.

**The signed form with blanks in it.** Your signature is the part you cannot take back, and the blanks above it can be filled in later with anything.

**The friendly questions.** Birthday, mother's maiden name, first school, the city you were born in. On a form they look like human resources doing its job. They are also the standing answers to account recovery questions, which chapter three takes further.

## The order is the tell

Real hiring has a shape. You talk to somebody, you get an offer you can read, carrying a company name and a person you can reach through a route you found yourself, and only then does anything with your ID on it move. Documents come after there is something to attach them to.

Reverse that order and the documents are the point. If the identity pack arrives before the interview, before a written offer, or before the company has a name you could look up on your own, the job is the wrapper and the pack is the product.

So do not become the applicant who refuses everything. Know the stages instead. At application: your resume, your samples, your links. At offer: your name as it appears on your ID, so a contract can be drawn up. At onboarding, once you hold a signed offer: the ID copies, the account details, the government numbers. Sending them then is normal, and refusing then would be strange. The stage is the whole question.

## The offer to receive and forward

Same week, different message. It is called payment coordinator, remittance officer, or finance assistant. A client will send money to your GCash or your bank, you keep a cut, you forward the rest the same day. There is no fee. The first transfers are real and you are paid on time.

This is not a job. What is being hired is your account and your name. Money that has to travel through a stranger's personal account is money that does not want to be traced, and the trail stops with the account holder, who is you. When the person it was taken from starts looking, your name is the one written on the transfer.

Nothing in the story changes that. Not a contract, not a company name, not screenshots of other coordinators being paid. An employer pays you for work. It does not need your account as a stop on the way to somewhere else.

## If you already sent them

You cannot un send a photo. What you can still do is treat everything in that pack as answers somebody now holds. Anything using your birthday, your mother's maiden name or your school as a recovery answer needs changing, and any account you named in the form needs its second step looked at. Keep the thread, the profile and the messages instead of deleting them in embarrassment. Chapter three walks the hour after, in order.

## Try this

Search your chat threads for the last photo of your ID you sent. Note who received it, what stage that process had reached, and whether you could reach that person today through a route you chose yourself. Write down the ones you would not send again.

lessons.title: The code and the number
lessons.content_mdx:
# The code and the number

A one time code is not a password and not a secret in the ordinary sense. It is the system stopping, turning to you, and asking whether you personally want this one thing to happen right now.

So reading a code to somebody does not tell them about the action. It hands them the action.

That is also why nobody who genuinely works at your bank, your wallet provider or a platform will ever ask you for one. They are already inside. The code exists to prove that you are.

## The scripts

**The fraud team calling you.** A transfer is being attempted right now, they are blocking it for you, a code is coming, read it back quickly. They use your name and maybe a recent transaction, which is easier to obtain than it feels and proves nothing about who is calling.

**The buyer who wants to verify you.** You are selling a phone on Marketplace. The buyer says the payment is sitting ready and will release once you confirm the code that just arrived. A buyer paying you needs nothing at all from your phone.

**The friend who cannot receive a code.** A message from an account you know. I am locked out, my number is not receiving, can I borrow yours, a code will arrive, just send it over. Your friend is not on the other end. That account was taken an hour ago and you are the next one on the list.

**The courier and the raffle.** A delivery to confirm, a prize to claim, a code to read back before either can be released.

## The tell that survives every script

The code message itself names the action it authorises. Open it and read it before you say anything.

If the message says the code will sign someone in, reset a password or add a device, and the caller says it will block a transfer, then one of them is lying and it is not the message. Remember also why the code arrived at all: somebody typed your number or your address into that flow seconds ago. An unrequested code is not a warning that someone might try. It is someone trying, now.

Chapter one gave you the habit, which is to end the call and reach the institution by a route you chose. This is where it earns its keep, because the pressure in these calls is deliberate. A caller who cannot let you hang up and ring back has answered your question for you.

## Your number is part of the lock

Once codes arrive by text, your number stops being a contact detail. It is a key. Whoever receives your codes can run the reset flows on their own: type your address into the forgotten password page, receive the code, set a new password, and be you.

Which gives an attacker a second route. Rather than getting a code out of you, they can arrange to receive your codes directly, by persuading whoever handles the process that they are you and that your number belongs on a SIM they are holding. What that process requires differs between providers and has changed before, so look yours up at the source rather than trusting a description in a chat. What matters here is the effect. Your codes now arrive somewhere else, and you were never asked.

## What it looks like from your side

Your phone quietly loses service in a place where you always have signal. Nobody beside you has the same problem. Calls and texts stop reaching you while the world still reaches your old number, so your friends notice nothing. Sometimes a flood of junk messages comes first, which is there to make you silence the phone or stop reading it.

Treat a dead phone as a takeover until you know otherwise. Two moves belong here and the rest is chapter three.

Do not start any reset that sends a code to that number, because you would be handing the reset to whoever holds it now. And get to another device and secure your mailbox first, since the mailbox is where every other reset lands.

## Where SMS sits

A code by text is the weakest of the real second factors, because it rides on the number and the number can be moved without you.

It is also much better than nothing. With it, a stolen password on its own stops being enough, and passwords are stolen in bulk from places you have no control over.

So the answer is never to switch it off and sit with a password alone. The answer is to move the accounts worth taking onto a second factor that does not depend on your number. Chapter three sets that out as a ladder and tells you how to find out where each of your own accounts can sit on it.

## Try this

Open the last one time code message you received. Read the sentence around the code and write down the action it names. That sentence is the one a caller will need you to ignore.

lessons.title: The permission you grant at install
lessons.content_mdx:
# The permission you grant at install

Dennis needs ₱4,000 before payday. Rent is short and his mother's maintenance medicine is due. He installs a lending app that promises approval in minutes. Before it shows him a single figure, it wants his contacts, his photo gallery and his messages.

He thinks he is deciding whether to borrow. He is deciding something larger and quieter, and he has about four seconds to do it while the loading screen waits.

## Why the app wants your phonebook

Lending is priced on the chance you repay. A lender looking at a borrower with no payslip, no collateral and no long record has to find its assurance somewhere.

When the app asks for your contacts and your gallery, that is where it found it. The permission is not a feature you receive. It is part of what you are paying with. Your phonebook is the leverage, and your gallery is what makes a message about you land harder.

Basic Finance carries the rest of that story: what the loan really costs once the rate is turned into pesos, what to do when you cannot pay, and where a complaint about a lender goes. This lesson is about the decision that comes before all of it, the one Dennis is making at the loading screen.

## What the leverage looks like when it is used

Dennis pays a day late. The messages do not go to Dennis.

They go to his sister, his old team leader, a client from two years ago, the number saved as Kuya Tricycle. Sometimes it is a group chat assembled out of his phonebook. Sometimes it is a photo from his gallery with words added to it.

That is what the permission bought. A lender who can only reach you has to deal with you. A lender who can reach everybody who knows you does not.

Paying does not reliably switch it off, because the pressure is the collection method rather than a step on the way to one.

And none of it is yours to absorb quietly. There is a line between collecting a debt and this, there is a regulator for the lending and another for the misuse of your contact list, and lenders operating here are required to be registered. Chapter three covers making the report and keeping every message while it happens.

## Match the permission to the job

One question, and it works on every app rather than only the lending ones.

What does this app do, and what would it need in order to do that?

A camera app needs the camera. A ride app needs your location while you are using it. A messaging app needs your contacts, because contacting people is the thing it does. A calculator, a wallpaper pack, a torch or a loan app asking for your phonebook is not being convenient. It is running a second business, and your contacts are its stock.

The mismatch is the whole signal. You do not have to work out what they intend to do with it. You only have to notice that the request does not fit the job.

## Say no before, not after

Deny it at the request rather than later in a settings review. Once you grant access to a list, a copy of that list can be taken in the first seconds. Revoking afterwards stops the next read. It does not reach back for the copy that already left your phone.

That makes install time the moment that counts. Installing something just to see what it offers has already made the decision, because the asking comes before the offering.

Your phone also gives you more answers than yes and no. Depending on the handset you may be able to allow something once, or only while the app is open, or choose individual photos instead of handing over the whole gallery. Look for those options where the request appears instead of assuming the choice is all or nothing.

And if an app refuses to open at all unless you give it something it has no use for, you have your answer. Close it.

## Audit what you already said yes to

Do this once a quarter, or the next time your phone feels slow. Go down your installed apps and ask three things of each.

Do I still use this one? The app from a single trip, the game a cousin recommended, the filter you opened once.

What does it hold? A gallery, a phonebook, a location history, a saved card, a scan of something.

What did I grant it, and would I grant that today?

Uninstall the dead ones and revoke what does not fit on the ones you keep. Being late does not make it pointless.

One thing this pass misses. The apps and sites you signed into using your email or your social account keep their access even after you delete the app from your phone, because that access lives on the account rather than on the handset. Chapter three handles those inside the hardening pass.

## Tell your own people, in your own words

If a phonebook has gone, the people in it are yours to warn, and hearing it from you first changes what they believe later. One line to the group chat does it. An app I installed has my contacts, so if anything about me reaches you from a number you do not know, it did not come from me, check with me first.

That sentence costs you nothing today and takes the sting out of anything that arrives later.

## Try this

Open your list of installed apps and pick the three you use least. For each one, write down what it can reach on your phone. Remove one of them today.

quiz.prompt: Marilou applies for home based encoding work. Two friendly messages later the recruiter says she is hired and sends an onboarding pack to fill in: a photo of her ID front and back, a selfie holding it, her bank account name and number, and a form to sign with blank fields. There has been no interview, no written offer, and no fee. What should she do?

options.text: Send the ID photo now but hold back the selfie and the account details until her first payday has actually arrived.
Send nothing yet, find the company through a route she chose herself, and confirm the role before any document moves.
Complete the pack, since no money is being asked for and identity documents are a normal part of onboarding anywhere.
Ask the recruiter for a company ID and a photo of their business permit first, then send the whole pack once those arrive.

quiz.explanation: The order is the tell. Documents come after there is something to attach them to: an interview, a written offer, a company you can reach on your own. Nothing here has a name she found herself. A company ID and a permit photo are images, and images are the easy part to produce. Splitting the pack still sends her ID, and waiting for a payday that never comes just means she sent it earlier.

quiz.prompt: A week ago Jomar sent a recruiter his ID photo, a selfie holding it, his last payslip and a form carrying his birthday and his mother's maiden name. The account has since vanished and the company has no trace anywhere he can find. What is the useful move now?

options.text: Message the account once more asking them to delete the files, and keep whatever reply comes back as proof.
Accept that nothing can be done once photos have been sent, and watch his bank balance carefully for a while.
Warn people in his job hunting group chat by name so nobody else in his batch sends the same pack over.
Treat those details as answers somebody now holds, and change anything that uses them for account recovery.

quiz.explanation: He cannot un send a photo, so the work now is limiting what the copy unlocks. His birthday, his mother's maiden name and his school are standing answers to recovery questions, and recovery is the back door into the accounts themselves. Asking a scammer to delete files gets a reassuring reply and nothing else. Warning the group is decent of him, but it protects other people rather than him.

quiz.prompt: Angel is offered work as a payment coordinator. A client sends money to her GCash, she keeps ₱500 of each transfer and forwards the rest the same day. There is no fee, no training kit, and the first two transfers really did pay her. What should she do?

options.text: Refuse the arrangement, because what is being hired here is her account, and the trail ends at her name.
Ask for a contract naming the company, then carry on if the paperwork looks proper.
Carry on but screenshot every transfer, so that she can show later she only forwarded what the client sent.
Take the work while it lasts, since none of her own money is at risk and the task itself is simple.

quiz.explanation: Money that has to travel through a stranger's personal account is money that does not want to be traced, and the account holder is the name on the transfer when somebody comes looking. A contract does not change whose account it is. Screenshots record her part in it rather than excusing it. Being paid on time and asked for nothing is what keeps the arrangement running.

quiz.prompt: Rico is selling a phone on Marketplace. The buyer says he has already paid and the wallet will release the money once Rico reads back the code that just landed on his phone, to confirm he is the real seller. The code message is sitting unopened. What is the right move?

options.text: Give the code to nobody and block the buyer, without opening the message the code came in.
Give the code to nobody and ask him to send the payment again, so a second code arrives to compare against the first.
Open the code message, act on the action it names rather than on the buyer, and give the code to nobody.
Give the code to nobody, and read one out only if a second message arrives from the wallet confirming him.

quiz.explanation: None of these hands the code over, so that is not what the question is about. The code message names the action it authorises, and reading that sentence is what breaks every version of this script, because no wallet needs a code from a seller before it releases a payment. Blocking without opening leaves Rico not knowing what was just attempted on his account, which is the thing that has actually happened. Asking for a second code invites a second attempt. Waiting for the wallet to confirm the buyer waits for a message a wallet does not send, and the one that arrives will be another text with a label on it.

quiz.prompt: A code lands on Nikko's phone at 9pm. He did not ask for one, nobody has called him, and the message says it will sign someone in to his e-wallet. He is about to ignore it and go to sleep. What should he do?

options.text: Treat it as somebody typing his details into the wallet sign-in now, and change that password tonight.
Reply STOP so no further codes reach his number, then look at the account properly in the morning.
Ignore it, since a code is only dangerous once somebody has heard it, and nobody has spoken to him at all.
Wait to see whether a second code arrives before he does anything, since one on its own may be a mistake.

quiz.explanation: An unrequested code is not a warning that somebody might try. It is somebody trying, now. The code exists because a person typed his address or his number into that sign-in seconds ago, which means they already hold something of his and are one step from the rest. Ignoring it leaves them there to try again with a better story. STOP is a reply to whoever arranged the sending, and it silences the alarm rather than the intruder. Waiting for a second code is waiting for the attempt to succeed. The code itself is safe while it stays on his phone, and the password behind it is the part somebody else already knows.

quiz.prompt: Kim's phone loses service mid afternoon in Quezon City where her signal is always fine, and her officemate on the same network has full bars. Her email and her wallet are both tied to that number. Her first instinct is to open her laptop and reset her email password. What should she do first?

options.text: Restart the phone and wait until the evening, since coverage drops out from time to time and comes back on its own.
Run the email password reset from the laptop now, so the code is waiting the moment signal comes back.
Message her contacts from the laptop to warn them that her number may no longer be reaching her at the moment.
Treat the number as taken and secure the mailbox from another device without sending any code to that number.

quiz.explanation: A phone that goes quiet while the phone beside it works is a takeover until proved otherwise. Any reset that sends a code to that number hands the reset to whoever holds it now, which makes it the worst available first move. Warning her contacts matters, but the mailbox holds the resets for everything else and it goes first.

quiz.prompt: Dennis installed a lending app three months ago and granted it his contacts, his photos and his messages. The loan is fully repaid and he has not opened the app since. What is worth doing now?

options.text: Leave it as it is, since the loan is settled and the permissions only mattered while he still owed money on the loan.
Revoke the permissions and then remove the app, while understanding that any copy taken earlier has already gone.
Revoke the permissions but keep the app installed, in case he needs another fast loan before a later payday.
Delete the app, which takes its access away along with everything it collected while it was installed.

quiz.explanation: Revoking stops the next read, and there is always a next read, so it is worth doing late. What it cannot do is reach back for the copy taken in the first seconds, and deleting the app does not retrieve that copy either. Keeping it installed for convenience keeps a live permission sitting on a phonebook that is not only his.

quiz.prompt: Pia installs a photo editing app a friend recommended. Before it will open at all, it asks for her gallery, her contacts and her messages. She is on a deadline for a client graphic. What should she do?

options.text: Grant all three now to get moving, then go back after the deadline and revoke whatever turns out to be unnecessary.
Grant the gallery and contacts but refuse messages, since sharing an edit needs a destination.
Grant only the gallery and treat the other two requests as a sign of what the app is really selling.
Grant everything, since an app with good reviews on the store has already been checked out by other people.

quiz.explanation: Match the permission to the job: editing photos needs photos, and nothing about the job explains contacts or messages. Granting now and tidying later gives away the copy, since revoking stops the next read rather than the last one. Reviews say people liked the editing, not what the app collected while they used it.
