lessons.title: Make the account expensive to take
lessons.content_mdx:
# Make the account expensive to take

Nobody can make an account impossible to take. What you can do is make it cost more than it is worth, so whoever is working through a list of stolen passwords gives up on your name and moves to the next one.

Do the pass in the order that protects the most value first: your email, then the accounts that hold or move money, then the social accounts that would speak in your voice to people who trust you.

## Email first, because email is the master key

Chapter one named the cascade. Whoever holds your mailbox holds the reset link for everything else, so one evening spent on your email is worth more than a week spent on the rest.

Nelia, a VA in Dumaguete, had a scare and spent a Saturday hardening her wallet and her Facebook. She left alone the free mailbox she opened in first year college and had not read since. That old address was still sitting there as the recovery email on her main mailbox. She had bolted the front door and left a key under the mat.

Harden every mailbox you own, including the abandoned one. If you genuinely cannot get back into an old address, then remove it from every account that still lists it.

## One password per account

A reused password means a break-in anywhere is a break-in everywhere. Somebody buys a password from a shopping site you forgot you joined, then tries the same email and password on your mailbox, then on your wallet. Nothing clever is happening. It is a list, tried in bulk, and a match costs the attacker nothing.

One password per account is only possible with a password manager, because you cannot hold thirty of them in your head. Judge one by what it does rather than by the brand or the price. It stores. It generates a long random password so you never have to invent another one. And it refuses to fill a login on an address it does not recognise, which is the free tripwire from chapter one: if the manager will not fill, read the address before you type anything.

Then set one up rather than reading about them. Install it on the phone and the browser you actually use. Set one long passphrase for the manager itself, several unrelated words, and write that one on paper at home, because it is the only password you now have to remember. Then move three accounts into it tonight, mailbox first, generating a new password for each as you go rather than saving the old one.

Long and unique beats clever and short. Several unrelated words you can actually type will hold up better than a short word with a few letters swapped for symbols, which adds far less than it feels like it does.

## The second factor is a ladder

A password on its own means one stolen string is the whole lock. A second factor means the thief needs the string and something else.

Climb as far as each account lets you:

1. Nothing at all.
2. A code sent to you by SMS.
3. A code from an authenticator app on your phone.
4. A passkey or a physical security key.

SMS sits low for the reason chapter two gave: whoever controls the number receives the codes, and a number can be taken. It still beats nothing by a distance, so if SMS is all an account offers, switch it on today instead of waiting for something better. Where an account offers an authenticator app or a passkey, climb. What each service supports keeps changing, so open the security settings of your own accounts and look, rather than trusting anybody's list, including this one.

## Recovery is the back door

People bolt the front and leave the back open. The recovery path is a second way into the same account, and it is usually the softer one.

On each account that matters, work through four things.

**The backup email.** Is it an address you still control and still read?

**The backup number.** Is it a number you still hold? A number you stopped paying for does not stay yours forever.

**The security questions.** Mother's maiden name, first school, first pet, the town you were born in. If the answer sits on your public profile, it is not a secret. Answer with something unrelated and store that answer in your password manager.

**The recovery codes.** Save them where a lost phone, a fire or a flood cannot take every copy at once. Printed and kept at home, plus one copy in your manager, is enough.

## Finish the pass

Changing a password does not evict somebody who is already inside. Close the leftovers they rely on:

- Sign out other sessions, on every device.
- Review connected apps and remove anything you do not recognise or no longer use.
- Check your mailbox for forwarding rules and filters. A rule quietly copying your mail to a stranger survives every password change you will ever make.

Do one account tonight, and make it your email. Password changed, second factor moved up a rung, recovery cleaned out, other sessions signed out, forwarding checked. Then put the next two accounts in your calendar for this week, and stop there. A pass you finish on three accounts beats a plan you abandon on twelve.

lessons.title: What you hand over, and to whom
lessons.content_mdx:
# What you hand over, and to whom

Marivic works nights at a call centre in Bacolod. Counting back through her chat threads, she has sent a photo of her ID eleven times this year: a room rental, a lending app, two raffles, a gym membership, a seller who wanted it before shipping, and five recruiters. She could not tell you where a single one of those copies is now, or who else has seen it.

None of that was a scam. That is the point. The exposure builds out of ordinary requests you said yes to without thinking, and the habit that fixes it is a standing one rather than a reaction to an obvious fraud.

## Three questions before anything leaves your hands

**Who is asking?** Not the name in the message, the organisation, and whether you went to them or they came to you.

**What is it for?** A specific step in a process you are actually in, or a vague requirement nobody has explained?

**What can they do with it if they are not who they say they are?** This is the question that changes behaviour, because it is the only one that assumes the answer to the first one might be a lie.

## Copies of your ID

Send the minimum. Send it at the stage of a process where it is normal, which is almost never the first message.

Mark the copy. Write across the image what it is for and the date, placed so the details the recipient legitimately needs stay readable. A copy that reads "for room rental application, 12 March" is harder to hand on for opening an account in your name somewhere else. Some organisations will ask for a clean copy instead, and that is a conversation to have with a named person at an organisation you approached, not with an account that messaged you first.

Treat the selfie holding your ID as a bigger ask than the ID by itself, because it exists to prove that a live person is holding that document. So does a short video of your face. When somebody wants both the document and the proof that you are standing behind it, they are assembling everything needed to be you.

## Your public profile is somebody's answer sheet

Your birthday with the year. Your mother's maiden name, in a comment under a family photo. The school and the year you left. The first pet, from a name-your-pet thread. The payslip photo. The boarding pass with the code printed on it. The new company ID posted the day you got hired, showing your full name, your employee number and where you work.

Each one is harmless. Together they answer the security questions from the last lesson and they hand a stranger enough detail to open a call sounding like somebody who already knows you.

The move is not to delete your life. It is to keep the answer set out of it: lock down what does not need to be public, stop answering the fun quizzes that are shaped exactly like recovery questions, and remember that your mother's maiden name is not a secret. It is a fact, and facts get looked up.

## Screen sharing and remote control

Nobody legitimate walks you through installing a remote control tool during a call. Not your bank, not a platform's support, not a courier, not a government office.

The reason is simple. Once it is installed, the person on the other end has your screen and often your keyboard, which means your mailbox, your wallet, and every code that arrives while they watch. If you are already in that call, end it, uninstall the tool, and treat it as an incident using the next lesson.

## Devices that are not only yours

The computer shop, the borrowed laptop, the family tablet, the office machine.

Assume a browser you do not own remembers what you type. Do not tick remember me. Sign out when you finish, and later, from your own device, sign out other sessions as well. Do not leave documents you care about sitting in a downloads folder on a machine somebody else uses. A family account whose password everyone knows is not an account with a password on it.

If you handle a client's material, the device holding it is part of your exposure and theirs. How you actually run client work belongs to the freelancing and client operations courses. What this course asks is narrower: the machine that file sits on should be yours, and hardened the way the last lesson describes.

## Do this today

Open your sent folder and your chat threads and search for your own attachments. Write the list of who currently holds a copy of your ID. You cannot pull those copies back, and that is not the point. The point is that the list stops growing tonight, because from now on nothing leaves your hands until you have answered the third question out loud.

lessons.title: The first hour
lessons.content_mdx:
# The first hour

Jerome, a freelancer in Antipolo, is on his phone at 11:40 at night when a login alert arrives from a city he has never visited. He taps through to change his password and it does not work. It has already been changed.

What follows is the checklist for that hour, written for somebody whose hands are shaking. The order matters more than the speed. The instinct is to run at the loudest problem, which is usually the money, and that is the wrong first move.

## 1. The mailbox, before anything else

Even when the visible loss is somewhere else. An attacker sitting inside your mailbox undoes every other fix you make, because every other fix ends in a reset link that lands there.

Change the mailbox password. Sign out all sessions. Then hunt the leftovers, which is the part people skip: recovery addresses and numbers that were added, forwarding rules, filters that quietly move warning mail out of your inbox, connected apps, and any app passwords issued to devices you do not recognise.

If you cannot get in at all, start the account's own recovery from a device you control. Read step 3 first if your phone has lost service.

## 2. Money, through a route you chose

Reach your bank or wallet the way chapter one taught: the app you installed yourself, the number printed on your card, a branch. Never the number in the message, and never a link somebody sent you. Say what happened and what you want done, and write down who you spoke to and when.

## 3. If the phone lost service, the number is taken

A phone that quietly drops to no service while the world still reaches your number is chapter two's tell, and in this hour you treat it as confirmed rather than possible.

Do not run any reset that sends a code to that number. You would be mailing the key to the person who took the lock. Use the routes that do not depend on it: a recovery code, an authenticator app on a device you still hold, a backup email. Then get to your provider in person, with your ID, and deal with the SIM before you trust that number again.

## 4. Capture the evidence before it disappears

Chat threads, the profile that contacted you, the page you typed into, the transaction, the alert emails. Screenshots with the time and date visible, plus the sender's name and the full address where you can see it. Save them somewhere that is not inside the compromised account, because messages get deleted and accounts get closed, sometimes within the hour.

Write a plain timeline while it is fresh: what arrived, when, what you did, what you clicked. You will not remember this clearly tomorrow.

## 5. Tell the people who will be targeted next

Your contacts, your clients, your employer. Chapter one said an account's value to a scammer is the trust it can borrow to reach the next person, and right now that next person is somebody who trusts you.

Say it plainly and quickly: this account is not mine at the moment, ignore anything sent from it, especially a request for money or for a code, and here is how to reach me instead. Send it from a channel they can verify is you. It is an uncomfortable message to write and it is the step that stops the loss spreading past you.

## 6. Report it

Take it to the institutions, and look up how to reach each one on the day, at the source, through an address you navigated to yourself:

- The platform or provider whose account was taken, through its own account security or fraud channel.
- Your bank or e-wallet's fraud channel.
- The Philippine cybercrime authorities, meaning the PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group and the NBI Cybercrime Division.
- The Securities and Exchange Commission, when an online lending app is the problem. Lending and financing companies operating here have to be registered with it, it publishes which ones are, and it takes complaints about how they collect. Look up its current complaint route on its own site on the day.
- The National Privacy Commission, where personal data has been misused. Between the two, the Privacy Commission takes the misuse of your contact list and your gallery, and the Securities and Exchange Commission takes the lender itself.

Channels, requirements and contact details change, so do not work from a number in a forwarded post. Keep every reference number you are given. Reporting is not the same thing as a refund request, and nobody can tell you in advance how one ends, so make the report and keep your own record either way.

## 7. The second wave

Weeks later somebody arrives offering to recover what you lost, for a fee paid upfront. It is the same crime finding you again, because being hit once put you on a list of people who can be reached. Pay nothing, keep the message, add it to your report. Basic Blockchain works through why a recovery offer of that shape cannot be what it says it is.

## Write your plan tonight

You will not compose this at midnight with your hands shaking. Take a sheet of paper now and number your own accounts in the order you would lock them, starting with the mailbox that holds the resets. Beside each one, write how you get in without your phone. Keep it somewhere you can reach without the account it protects.

quiz.prompt: Marlon uses a password manager, a different password on every account, and an authenticator app on his mailbox. That same mailbox still lists a school address he lost access to years ago as its recovery email, and its security answers are his real first school and his real first pet, both of which appear on his public profile. What gives him the biggest gain now?

options.text: Replace the stale recovery address and change the security answers to unrelated strings he stores.
Set an even longer password on the mailbox, since that is the account every other reset runs through.
Add a second authenticator app on the same phone so he has a backup if the first one stops working.
Switch off the SMS option on the mailbox so nobody can reach it by taking over his phone number.

quiz.explanation: He has hardened the front door and left the back one open. A recovery address he cannot open is an address somebody else may be able to claim, and security answers that are published facts are not answers, they are lookups. A longer password does nothing for a path that never asks for the password, a second authenticator on the same phone shares the same single point of failure, and turning off SMS on an account that already uses an app removes an option without closing the recovery hole.

quiz.prompt: Ann-Margaret sells shoes online and has an authenticator app on her seller account. Somebody calls saying they are from the platform's seller support, knows her store name and her last two orders, and says her verification keeps failing: she should turn the second factor off for ten minutes so their system can relink the account, and they will tell her when to switch it back on. What should she do?

options.text: Tell the caller she will not switch it off, stay on the line, and hear out what the relink needs.
Tell the caller she will not switch it off, then search the platform's help pages and follow the relink steps she finds.
Leave it switched on and take a reference number and a callback number from her, then ring that number back to go on.
Leave it switched on, end the call herself, and go back to seller support through the app she installed.

quiz.explanation: All four refuse to lower the factor, so the question is what happens next. Staying on the line keeps her inside a conversation that opened with a request to disable her lock, and a callback number she was handed is the caller's number whichever end dials it. Searching for help pages is closer and it is still not a route she chose, since a paid slot can sit above the real one. Knowing her store name and recent orders proves nothing, because order details reach buyers, sellers and anybody reading a screen over a shoulder. She ends the call herself and comes back through the app she installed, which is the only one of the four that nobody arranged for her.

quiz.prompt: Erwin learned this week that SMS codes are the weakest second factor. His mailbox offers an authenticator app, and his e-wallet offers codes by SMS and nothing else. He is about to switch the SMS codes off on the wallet because he no longer trusts them. What should he do?

options.text: Switch SMS off on both accounts, since a code that can be intercepted is worse than having no code at all.
Keep the wallet on SMS for now, and move the mailbox up to the authenticator app it already offers.
Leave both on SMS and rely on a long unique password at the wallet instead of a second factor.
Switch the wallet's codes off now and turn them back on if it ever starts offering an app.

quiz.explanation: The ladder runs from nothing, to SMS, to an authenticator app, to a passkey or a physical key, and every rung beats the one below it. SMS is weak because whoever holds the number holds the codes, but removing it drops the wallet to a single stolen password, which is worse. Climb where climbing is possible and stay put where it is not. A long password is the first factor, not a second one.

quiz.prompt: A landlady in Cavite messages Kristine on chat about a room she advertised. Before Kristine has seen the unit, met her, or agreed to anything, the landlady asks for a photo of the front and back of her ID, a selfie holding it, and a copy of her latest payslip. What should Kristine do?

options.text: Send the ID but hold back the selfie and the payslip, since those are the parts that matter.
Ask which agency she works with, then send all three once that answer sounds convincing enough to her.
Send nothing yet, view the room first, and hand over ID when a contract is actually being signed.
Send all three with the numbers blurred, so a stolen copy cannot be used to open anything.

quiz.explanation: The question is not only what to send but at which stage, and this stage is a chat with a stranger about a room nobody has viewed. Documents plus a selfie holding them is the full set needed to be you somewhere else. An agency name offered over chat is not a check, and blurring numbers still hands over your face, your name and proof you were holding the document. When the process reaches a signing, send the minimum and mark the copy with what it is for and the date.

quiz.prompt: Rommel wakes to a wallet alert for a transfer of ₱6,000 he did not make. He opens his mailbox to find the confirmation email and it is not there, and neither is anything else from the last three days. He starts by changing his wallet password. What should he do instead?

options.text: Carry on: change the wallet password and the PIN, then watch the balance for the rest of the morning.
Stop and secure the mailbox first: new password, sign out all sessions, then clear the leftovers.
Report the transfer to the wallet provider and deal with the mailbox once somebody has replied.
Uninstall and reinstall the wallet app so any session on another device is cut off immediately.

quiz.explanation: Three days of missing mail says somebody is inside the mailbox, probably with a filter hiding the alerts. Every wallet fix he makes ends in a reset link that lands in that mailbox, so the wallet work is undone as fast as he does it. Mailbox first: password, all sessions out, then the forwarding rules, added recovery addresses and connected apps. Reinstalling an app does not end a session held on another device, and waiting on a reply is time the attacker keeps.

quiz.prompt: Cherry's phone drops to no service at two in the afternoon and does not recover. On her laptop she finds she has been signed out of her mailbox. The reset page offers three routes: a code to her number, a recovery code, or a link to her backup email. Which route should she take?

options.text: Send the code to her number and ask a friend to try calling her to see whether the line works.
Send the code to her number anyway, since the mailbox is the account to save first.
Wait for the signal to come back before touching any reset, so the process is not interrupted.
Treat the number as taken, reset with a recovery code, and fix the SIM before using it.

quiz.explanation: A phone that quietly loses service while the number still works for everybody else is the tell that somebody else is now receiving your codes. Sending a reset code there hands them the mailbox as well, and a test call tells her nothing useful in time. Waiting costs her the hour that matters. She uses a route the number cannot touch, then sorts the SIM out in person before trusting it again.

quiz.prompt: Alvin gets his Messenger account back after an hour. Nothing of his own was taken, but while it was gone the attacker sent an urgent request for money to dozens of his contacts, two of them clients. He has already changed the password and signed out other sessions. What should he do now?

options.text: Message the contacts who were written to, from a channel they know is him, saying what to ignore.
Say nothing now, since the account is his again and telling people will only worry them for nothing.
Report the account to the platform and let it warn the people who received those messages.
Post about it publicly later in the week, once he is sure nobody else has been affected.

quiz.explanation: The account was worth taking because of the trust it could borrow, and that trust is being spent on his contact list right now. Recovering the account does not unsend a request for money to a client. A platform does not warn his contacts for him, and a public post next week arrives after anybody who was going to pay has paid. He tells the people at risk, quickly, through something they can verify is him.

quiz.prompt: Two weeks after losing ₱18,000 to a fake buyer, Marites gets a message from an account offering to recover it. They post screenshots of money returned to other victims and ask for a processing fee upfront, which they say is refundable once her funds land. What should she do?

options.text: Pay nothing, block the account, and delete the message so she is not tempted by it later in the week.
Pay nothing yet, and ask them to recover it first and take their fee out of whatever comes back.
Pay nothing, keep the message and the account name, and add both to the report she has already made.
Pay nothing, and post the account name in her sellers' group chat so the next person gets a warning.

quiz.explanation: None of these pays the fee, which is the easy half. Somebody who knows she was hit knows it because being hit put her on a list, so the message is evidence about the first crime as well as an attempt at a second. Deleting it destroys the only thing she has gained from the whole exchange, and blocking without keeping it does the same. Asking them to work first accepts that there is a recovery to negotiate about and keeps the conversation open, which is what the fee was really for. Warning her group is decent of her and does nothing about her own report. She keeps it, hands it to the institutions she already reported to, and answers nothing further.

final_exam.title: Online Safety and Scam Defence final exam

questions.prompt: A number you did not know messaged you in June, apologised for the wrong number, and stayed. You have talked most days since: your job hunt, her business, your families. She has never asked you for money. This week she mentions that her uncle runs a small private group for Filipina traders, and that to be added you send a photo of your ID and a selfie holding it. What should you do?

options.text: Send neither, and ask her uncle to explain how the group actually works first, so you know what you would be joining.
Send neither, and tell her you will join once you have met her in person on her next trip home.
Send neither and take it no further, since the months were the approach and the documents are the point.
Send neither, block her, and delete the thread, since anybody running that approach will just move on to the next name.

questions.explanation: A slow approach spends months buying something a fast one cannot: your belief that this person is ordinary. The tell is not the story, it is the shape. No offer for months, then a first ask that is not money but identity. A photo of an ID together with a selfie holding it is the pair used to prove that you are you, which is exactly why it is worth collecting, and once sent it cannot be taken back. All four options hold the documents, so what separates them is what you do with the conversation. Asking the uncle to explain and setting a condition for later both keep you inside a script that has been answering smoother questions than yours for months, and a meeting that is always one trip away is the oldest part of the pattern. Blocking is sensible and deleting the thread is not: months of messages are the record of how you were approached, and this course asks you to keep exactly that. Whether the trading returns can be real is a Basic Finance question and it does not need answering here, because the documents were the loss.

questions.prompt: Your freelancing profile shows the payout account changed on Tuesday to a bank you have never used, and two invoices worth ₱11,200 between them have already been marked paid to it. Your own wallet and bank are untouched. You search your mailbox for the platform's change-of-details notice and it is not there, though older mail from the same platform is. You have twenty minutes before your shift. What do you do first?

options.text: Secure the mailbox first: new password, sign out every session, then clear any forwarding rule, filter or recovery address that was added.
Reach the platform through the app you installed and ask for the payouts to be reversed, then work the mailbox once somebody answers.
Change the payout account back on the profile and reset its password, then get to the mailbox once the profile is locked.
Message the two clients whose invoices were paid into that account, since they are the ones out of pocket and they need to hear it from you tonight.

questions.explanation: One notice missing while older mail from the same sender sits there is not the platform failing to write. It is somebody inside the mailbox moving it, with a filter or a forwarding rule, and that makes the mailbox the compromised account whatever the visible loss looks like. Nothing was taken from your wallet, and that is the part that misleads: the rule is mailbox first even when the money went somewhere else, because every fix you make anywhere else ends in a reset link landing there. Lock the profile first and whoever holds the mailbox resets it back within the hour. Reaching the platform is right and it is the second move rather than the first. The clients do need telling, and telling them before you have closed the door means telling them twice.

questions.prompt: You run a small online store from one mailbox, protected by an authenticator app. The bookkeeper you hired for the month says the codes are slowing her down and asks you to switch that mailbox back to text codes and share the password with her for the two weeks she is pulling statements. What should you do?

options.text: Keep the password to yourself, and move that mailbox onto text codes for the fortnight so the app stops holding her up.
Keep the mailbox as it is and get her the statements another way, since her work never needs the keys to your resets.
Keep the password to yourself, and set a rule forwarding the bank's mail to her address until the work is done.
Keep the password to yourself, and read her the code out of the app each time she needs to sign in during the fortnight.

questions.explanation: A protection does not have to be defeated if the owner can be talked into lowering it, and a plausible reason is what does the talking. None of these hands over the password, and three of them hand over something just as useful. Moving that mailbox back to text codes drops it onto your phone number, which is the one part of the lock somebody can take without ever touching you. Reading a code aloud is the same act the fraud caller wants, wearing a friendlier face, and the code authorises whatever was typed in seconds earlier rather than whatever you were told. A forwarding rule is the exact leftover an attacker installs, and it copies your mail out of the account for as long as nobody remembers to remove it. She needs documents. Send documents.

questions.prompt: Your cousin installed a loan app last month. It approved her in minutes, and at install it asked for her contacts, her photos and her messages, and she tapped allow on all three. She has not missed a payment. What should you tell her to do?

options.text: Uninstall the app today, which pulls back its access along with the copy of the contact list it took while the permission was live.
Pay the balance off early, which closes the arrangement and with it any reason for the app to reach anyone in her phone at all.
Leave the permissions as they are until the loan is cleared, since taking access away now is what makes a lender treat a borrower as a risk.
Turn off the permissions it does not need, check the same permissions on other apps she kept, and tell her own contacts in her own words.

questions.explanation: Access to contacts, photos and messages is not a convenience for a loan app. It is the product, because your reputation with the people in your phone is what the collection runs on. Revoking stops what happens next and does not reach a copy already taken, which is why she tells her own people first and in her own words rather than letting them hear it from a stranger. Uninstalling has the same limit and gets sold as a fix. Paying early is a decision about the loan, not about the copy. What the loan actually costs, and what to do about collection messages once they start, are Basic Finance's.

questions.prompt: A client you have worked with for eight months emails you. The shared folder has moved, here is the link, sign in with your work email to keep your access. The sender address matches the one she has always used, it sounds like her, and she did mention last week that they were changing systems. What should you do?

options.text: Do not use the link, and reply to her asking her to confirm she sent it before you go looking for the folder.
Do not use the link, and open the folder from your own bookmark first, then follow the link if it really has gone.
Do not use the link. Open the folder the way you always have, and message her on the number you already use if it has moved.
Do not use the link, and forward the mail to a colleague on the same account so he can open it and say whether it is genuine.

questions.explanation: This message is probably genuine, and that is the point of the item. All four refuse the link, so the question is what you do instead, and two of them start from a route you already had. A reply goes to whoever is holding that mailbox, so it confirms nothing. Checking your bookmark and then following the link anyway is the habit and its opposite in one move: a folder that really has moved does not make the link genuine, and the page it opens still wants the password that gets somebody everything. Opening the link on a colleague's account spends his password instead of yours and answers nothing, because a page built to harvest one does not misbehave visibly. Arriving by a route you already had costs you nothing on the day the message is real, and reaching her on the number you already use is the second half of the same habit.

questions.prompt: Your phone has had no signal since you woke up, and your sister's phone on the same network in the same room is fine. Your laptop is still signed in to your mailbox and nothing there has been changed yet. What do you do first?

options.text: Get to the operator branch with your ID and sort the SIM out, since nothing you change holds while somebody else takes your codes.
Change the passwords on your wallet and your bank from the laptop, since the number can complete a reset on either of them.
Run the mailbox's own recovery from the laptop for a clean sign-in, taking whichever verification route the page offers first.
Use the mailbox session you still hold: change the password, sign out other devices, and take that number off its recovery.

questions.explanation: One phone dead while another beside it on the same network works means the loss of service is yours rather than the network's, and your number is part of the lock on everything that texts you a code. What you also have is a signed-in session on a device nobody has touched, and that is the asset with a clock on it, since it ends the moment somebody resets the account from the other side. Use it while it is there. A recovery flow started from the laptop is a fresh sign-in you do not need, and the route it offers first may be a code to the number you no longer hold. The wallet and the bank come after the mailbox, because the mailbox holds the reset link for both of them. The operator and the SIM are the same day's work and not the first ten minutes of it.

questions.prompt: One password with a number on the end covers your email, two wallets, Facebook and a dozen shopping accounts. One of those shops was breached last year and you changed nothing at the time. You have this evening free and no idea where to start. Where should you start?

options.text: Set a new and longer version of that same password everywhere, so every account moves off the breached one in a single sitting tonight.
Start at the mailbox: a password nothing else uses, plus a second factor that is not your phone number, then the money accounts after it.
Start at the two wallets, since that is where the money actually sits, and work through the email and the shops over the next few weekends.
Turn on text-message codes across all of them tonight and leave the passwords, since a stolen password on its own is then not enough.

questions.explanation: The mailbox holds the reset link for everything else, so it is not one account among many and it is not where you finish. Harden the wallets first and whoever holds the mailbox simply resets them back. A longer version of the same password is still one password: the breached shop tells an attacker your pattern, and a pattern used everywhere still turns one break-in into all of them. Codes by text beat nothing and sit low on the ladder, since the number can be taken, and they do nothing at all about a password already circulating from last year's breach.

questions.prompt: A recruiter in a group chat gave you product-rating work. Two payouts of ₱350 arrived on time. Before the bigger batch she asks for a photo of your ID, a selfie holding it, your bank account name and number, and a form to sign with the salary line left blank. What should you do?

options.text: Send none of it, since paid work needs neither a selfie holding your ID nor a signed blank, and that set opens things in your name.
Send none of it yet, and ask for the bigger batch to be paid up front, so nothing with your face on it moves before you have been paid.
Send none of it yet, and ask her to fill in the salary line first, since a completed form is safe enough to sign and return.
Send none of it, and offer a certificate of employment from your last job instead, which shows who you are without a selfie.

questions.explanation: Payouts that arrive are not proof of an employer, and Basic Finance covers why an early payment is worth making. All four hold the pack, so the question is whether the request is worth negotiating with at all. A filled-in salary line does not make a signature safe when the rest of the form is still somebody else's to complete. Asking to be paid first treats the money as the risk, and here the documents are the risk. A certificate of employment is not a smaller ask: it carries your employer, your salary, your employee number and a signature block, which is a clean template to copy. What this course owns is what the paperwork is for. An ID copy, a selfie holding it and an account in your name are the pieces used to open something, borrow something, or route somebody else's stolen money through your account, which puts your name on the case rather than theirs.

questions.prompt: You reach a second interview with an agency you found and checked yourself. The day before, the coordinator asks you to send a photo of your ID, a selfie holding it, a copy of your last payslip, and a photo of your ATM card. What should you do?

options.text: Send nothing yet, ask what each item is for, and send only the ID at the stage where it is normal, marked with purpose and date.
Send nothing until the interview is over, then send all four, since by then the agency has decided and the stage is a normal one.
Send nothing, and later send only the ID and the payslip, since the selfie and the card are the ones that could be used against you.
Send nothing yet, and send whatever she asks for once she has confirmed in writing that the agency needs all four items.

questions.explanation: A real employer does not stop a list from being wrong, and this one is wrong: a photo of an ATM card and a payslip have no use in hiring at any stage, which says the list was written by somebody collecting rather than somebody hiring. All four hold something back, so the discrimination is on the list itself rather than on the refusing. Waiting until after the interview still sends the card. Holding back the selfie and the card still sends a payslip, which carries your employer, your salary, your employee number and a signature block, and none of that is needed to interview you. A written confirmation from the person doing the asking tests nothing, since she is the one you are unsure about. Three questions run before anything leaves your hands: who is asking, what is it for, and what can they do with it if they are not who they say. Marking a copy with what it is for and the date makes it harder to reuse somewhere else.

questions.prompt: You have reported a takeover to the platform and to your e-wallet's fraud channel. The wallet read you a reference number over the phone, the platform gave you a case number in a chat window you have since closed, and you have written nothing down. It is one in the morning and you are exhausted. What should you do before you sleep?

options.text: Sleep, and put it all together in the morning when you are clearer, since nothing is going to move overnight anyway.
Write to both organisations asking them to resend the reference numbers, and start your record once their replies arrive.
Write the numbers down now, beside a plain timeline of what arrived when and what you did, kept outside the accounts involved.
Save the timeline as a draft in the mailbox it all refers to, so it sits alongside the alert emails and the messages themselves.

questions.explanation: Reference numbers are the only handle you have on a report once the call ends, and a case number in a closed chat window is a case number you no longer hold. The timeline is worth more than it looks: what arrived, when, what you did, what you clicked, written while it is fresh, because tomorrow you will remember the feeling and not the order. Asking both organisations to resend puts your own record in somebody else's queue and starts it days late. A draft in the mailbox that was taken lives inside the account that may still not be yours, where it can be read or deleted by whoever is in there. Sleeping on it is the one thing the hour after a takeover does not allow, because the details you will need are the ones that go first.

questions.prompt: Your main mailbox has a password nothing else uses and an authenticator app on it. Its recovery address is a free webmail account you opened in first year: still yours, still on the password you set back then, and not signed into for four years. What should you do?

options.text: Harden the old mailbox the way you hardened this one, unique password and a second factor, or take it off recovery instead.
Take the old address off recovery straight away, since an address you never read is a route you have no way to watch.
Leave it, since an address you still control is not a hole, and a recovery route you own beats having no route at all.
Set the old address to forward everything to the main mailbox, so anything landing there reaches you where you actually read.

questions.explanation: Recovery is the back door, and the question is not only whether you control the old address but whether anything is defending it. A free mailbox on a password you set as a first year, unread for four years, is the softest account you own, and it holds a reset link into the one you just spent an evening hardening. Chapter three's rule runs harden every mailbox you own, including the abandoned one, and remove it only if you genuinely cannot get back in. You can get back in, so the work is real rather than a deletion. Taking it off is not wrong and it is second best, because it closes a route without the account behind it becoming any safer. Forwarding is worse than it looks: it shows you what arrives and leaves the old mailbox exactly as takeable as it was, and whoever takes it still runs the reset.

questions.prompt: A text arrives in the same thread as every genuine alert your bank has ever sent you, sitting above them and below them. It says a device was added to your account and gives a link to remove it if it was not you. The older messages in that thread are real, and the ₱24,000 transfer limit it quotes is the one you actually have. What is the read on this?

options.text: The thread is real, so the sender is real, and the only open question left is whether a device really was added to it.
The thread tells you only that the label matched, so nothing is verified, and you check the account in your app.
The correct limit settles it, since a stranger could not know a figure that sits inside the account.
It is safe to act on, since it asks you only to remove something rather than to send money or hand anything over.

questions.explanation: The name printed above a message is a label, and labels get set. A message that lands inside the thread holding your real alerts tells you the label matched, which is what the trick is for, and says nothing at all about who sent it. Your limit, your last transaction and your branch leak, get bought, or sit on a receipt, so a correct detail is a cost the sender paid rather than proof of anything. Remove-a-device is the friendlier wrapper on the same request, because the page it lands on asks you to sign in first, and signing in is the whole point. There is no reading of this message that gets you to the truth, which is why the habit is not to read harder. You open the app you installed and look, and that costs you a minute whether the alert was real or not.

questions.prompt: You have just moved your email and both wallets off text codes and onto an authenticator app on your phone. The setup screen hands you a list of one-time recovery codes and asks you to keep them somewhere safe. What should you do with them?

options.text: Write them out and keep the paper in your wallet, so it is on you whenever you have to sign in from somewhere new.
Email them to yourself, so that they stay searchable from any device you can still sign in from later on.
Screenshot them into your gallery so they travel with you on the same phone that holds the authenticator app.
Write them out and keep that copy at home, plus one in your manager, so that no single loss takes them all.

questions.explanation: Recovery codes exist for the day the phone is gone, so any copy living on that phone is gone with it, and the gallery is also what an app you gave photo access to can read. Emailing them puts the way back into every account inside the one account that already holds the reset link for all of them, so a taken mailbox becomes a taken everything. Two of these are off the phone and only one of them survives the day you need it: paper in your wallet travels with the phone, is lost with the bag, and is soaked by the same rain. The requirement is not simply off the phone. It is that no single loss, theft, fire or flood takes every copy at once.

questions.prompt: Your shop's page was taken for six hours yesterday and you have it back. While it was gone it sent two customers a payment account that is not yours, and one of them paid ₱3,900 into it. You have already told both of them and changed everything on your side. The customer who paid asks you what she should do now. What do you tell her?

options.text: That the loss is yours to carry, so you will refund her today and there is nothing further she needs to do about it.
To report it to her own bank or wallet's fraud channel now and keep the reference, since it left her account.
To message the account she paid and ask for the money back, since the transfer is recent.
To wait until the platform finishes looking into the page, since its findings are what any bank will ask her for first.

questions.explanation: The money left her account, so the fraud channel that can do anything about it is her bank's or her wallet's, not yours and not the platform's, and speed is the whole variable in whether a transfer can still be reached. She keeps the reference number, because it is the only handle she will have on that report next week. Messaging the account she paid tells whoever holds it that the payment landed and that she is worth another message. Waiting for the platform's findings spends the hours that matter on a report she does not need in order to make her own. Refunding her may well be the right thing for your shop, and it is a separate decision from hers: telling her that nothing further is needed costs her the report she should be making tonight.

questions.prompt: The recovery questions on one of your accounts are your mother's maiden name, your first school and your first pet. Your Facebook carries a birthday post naming your mother, your school sits in your intro, and years ago you answered a tag game naming the pet. What should you do?

options.text: Set the whole profile to friends only, which puts those posts out of reach of anybody who is not already a contact of yours today.
Treat the answers as public, and move that account's recovery onto a backup phone number of yours instead of questions.
Treat the answers as public now, and replace them with strings that are not true and are stored the way a password is stored.
Leave the answers and rely on the second factor instead, since a second factor covers the account whatever a question says.

questions.explanation: A security question is a password you already told everybody, and this is the same profile that feeds the approach in the first place. Once something has been posted, treat it as known: it can be screenshotted, saved, or read by the friend whose own account is taken next year. Friends only helps what you post next and not what has been up for years. Two of these do treat the answers as public, and only one of them closes the door. Moving recovery onto a number swaps a question anybody can look up for a number anybody can take, which is the piece a SIM swap goes after, so the back door is still a back door. A second factor is worth having, and recovery is a path around it, which is why an answer that is not true and is stored the way a password is stored is the fix.
